newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore jet fuel at pre-winter high on Iraq news.
newsitem.headline: Singapore jet fuel at pre-winter high on Iraq news.

text.p: Jet fuel prices in Singapore have soared to a year's high on the back of high crude prices as tension in Iraq mounts, trading sources said on Tuesday.
Paper jet fuel for September traded several times late at $29.50 to 29.60 per barrel on Monday as refiners sold to hedge their product sales at the higher values.

Based on this paper value, and the prevailing premium of more than 40 cents per barrel to Singapore spot quotes, refiners are able to sell their jet fuel at more than $30 per barrel free-on-board (fob) Singapore basis, one trader said.

The crudes and products markets rallied on Monday after the United Nations postponed its oil-for-food deal with Iraq following the incursion of Baghdad's troops into Kurdish areas of north Iraq in support of one of the region's warring factions.
Both markets jumped further on Tuesday morning on reports that U.S. B-52 bombers carrying cruise missiles were in the air from bases in Guam. It was not known if they were headed for Iraq.
Singapore jet fuel prices peaked earlier this year at close to $34 per barrel in early January as a second round of purchases for an expectedly cold winter then drove prices up.
Brokers said it was highly unusual for jet fuel prices to be at current levels at this time of the year and were half expecting of a price correction.
They cited high stocks in Guam and a stock build-up in Singapore and the MidEast as other reasons for a possible downward price change.
But traders were confident that prices would be kept firm by higher values in the West which would keep arbitrage cargoes out of this market.
In fact, in a rare instance, at least one jet fuel cargo was seen moving to the U.S. West Coast during end-August because values there were higher.
They said any further rise in U.S./Iraq tension would boost prices.
Traders were also confident of firmer prices as the market enters the fourth quarter, traditionally the strongest period as winter demand picks up.
